editorial:
Imagine gathering with your siblings for a big birthday party, but instead of cake and hugs, you get a loud shouting match about things that happened thirty years ago. That is exactly what happens here. You follow a liberal professor and his two sisters who come back together for their father's 75th birthday right before the 9/11 attacks. The vibe is tense and awkward, like a family dinner where someone finally brings up the one topic everyone agreed to ignore. You will see how three people can grow up in the same house but remember their childhood in completely different ways, leading to some really funny but mean arguments.

The acting is the best part because the actors make the fighting feel real and raw. While the movie is mostly just people talking in a room, the sharp dialogue keeps you interested in who is lying and who is telling the truth. It might feel a bit slow if you want big action, but if you love character studies, it is a win.
endingExplained: As the movie wraps up, the siblings finally stop fighting and admit that their memories of their father are flawed. They realize that holding onto old anger is only hurting them. They decide to forgive each other and start over, choosing a new beginning over old grudges. The timing is sad because you know the world is about to change forever with 9/11, making their small family peace feel even more important and fragile.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves family dramas and strong dialogue.
